headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading-error pathways exist because dexter’s autonomous API/file use can consume argo-workflows outputs, while both agents touch sensitive data classes and lack documented isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can emit workflow artifacts via APIs and B can read/write a scratchpad and act autonomously, so A’s outputs could be treated as instructions if bridged through files or copied text. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred from both profiles rather than observed.
conditions: IF A’s workflow output is copied into B’s scratchpad or prompt context
IF an operator bridges the agents through shared files or pasted text
mitigations: Keep a strict human review step before B consumes A outputs
Separate A and B into different directories
Strip instructions from A outputs before passing them onward
Use a fixed schema for A-to-B handoff
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all handoff artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches artifacts and parameters and has allowlisted egress; B touches financial and market data and calls multiple external APIs. If they share a workspace or handoff files, sensitive data can flow from one agent into the other’s outbound requests. The shared-workspace pathway is not documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem or scratch directory
IF B is given artifacts containing sensitive parameters or financial data
mitigations: Store A and B outputs in separate directories
Disable automatic upload of shared files to external APIs
Redact sensitive fields before handoff
Review B API calls for embedded file contents
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can call REST/gRPC APIs and B can call several external APIs with autonomous execution and multiple instances. Their overlapping networked write surfaces can conflict on shared mutable resources or rate-limited services, especially if both target the same backend. No locking or coordination is documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external API-backed resource
IF B runs multiple instances against the same shared service without coordination
mitigations: Assign disjoint API credentials per agent
Serialize writes to shared backends
Add per-resource locking in the orchestrator
Throttle concurrent runs of B
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s autonomous execution and API access make it likely to act on A’s outputs without strong verification unless an explicit review step exists. A produces workflow artifacts, and B can turn those into downstream actions or API calls, creating a classic unverified handoff with potentially broad impact.
conditions: IF A’s outputs are used as inputs to B without validation
IF B is allowed to execute actions based on A-generated artifacts
mitigations: Insert a human approval gate between A and B
Require B to validate A outputs against source data
Limit B to read-only analysis mode
Log and diff all A-to-B handoffs
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: A touches artifacts and parameters, while B touches financial and market data and requests many third-party API keys. If EU or regulated financial data flows into B’s external APIs, the pair can create a compliance breach through uncontrolled cross-border or third-party processing. No residency or DPA controls are documented, so uncertainty escalates.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is processed by B’s external APIs
IF any residency or retention requirement applies to the shared data
mitigations: Block regulated data from B’s API calls
Review vendor DPAs and residency terms
Minimize retained logs and scratch files
Tag regulated datasets before handoff
requires-engineering: enforce policy-based data routing
